newsitem.title: UK: Analysts discount impact of Australia cane damage.
newsitem.headline: Analysts discount impact of Australia cane damage.

text.p: Reports that 20 percent of Australia's sugar cane crop suffered cyclone damage could benefit other suppliers in the longer term but had failed to affect world markets, analysts said on Monday.
More time would be needed to assess the impact of cyclone Justin, which flattened cane across widespread areas of the main growing district of northeast Queensland over the weekend, they said.
"It's not good news, that's for sure," said one London-based analyst.
"But cane is fairly resilient -- it may have been damaged but it doesn't mean they're going to lose 20 percent of their crop," she said.

Although some market sources forecast a spike higher on the New York raw sugar futures market, saying the nearby May contract could surge to 13.00 cents/lb, activity was subdued and it opened unchanged at 10.83.

Other analysts said while Australia might see some short-term disruptions when crushing begins in June, the actual impact of reduced supply on prices was difficult to gauge as futures trading has been on the thin side in recent weeks.
"You have to have somebody putting their money in volume on that, and that really comes down to the funds," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar.

Any market impact would necessarily be delayed while the various buyers contracted to buy sugar from Queensland Sugar Corporation (QSC) assessed whether they might have to find alternative suppliers, he said.

"Presumably the buyers who have Queensland contracts at the moment don't feel sufficiently panicked, or at least haven't got any hard information, to go rushing out and buy something else," Pack said.

QSC chief executive David Rutledge said after addressing an industry conference in Brisbane on Monday that cyclone damage to the current crop would need to be very extensive for it to affect world prices.
Justin, the first cyclone to seriously hit Australia's sugarcane crop since the 1970s, landed as Australia was in the final months before the cane crush, which begins in June and runs to December.
Analysts said South Africa was the most likely candidate to benefit from any reduction in Australia's 1997/98 raw sugar production.

Although Thailand was in the same geographical area, it was not a direct competitor with Australia as it normally sold its sugar in the first half of the calendar year whereas Australia sold in the second, they said.

"It would benefit them (Thailand) to the extent that they have raw sugar they are holding back," Pack said, adding that Thailand would not normally have sugar available from the new cane crop until the year's end.

In its latest revision to world production estimates, Czarnikow Sugar said Australia would turn out 5.62 million tonnes of sugar raw value in the 1996/97 crop year, up from the 5.13 million produced in 1995/96.
